title: Renew our days (Lamentations 5:21)
hookLine: the book's closing plea, "renew our days as of old", sung as the Torah returns to the ark
carry: a plea that has already been through the worst

cards: Some books end on a wedding, some on a homecoming. Lamentations ends on a verse that's hard to say out loud in a room full of mourners. The line just before it has had a longer life.

Two weeks ago, this path heard the tree-of-life verses sung as the Torah scroll goes back into the ark. Right after them, as the doors close, comes this line, lifted from the last page of a book of ruins.

teach.h: TURN US, AND WE SHALL BE TURNED.
teach.b: Renew our days. The verse in full, in the JPS 1917 translation: "Turn Thou us unto Thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; Renew our days as of old." In Hebrew it begins hashivenu: turn us, bring us back.
First, turn us. Not, we will turn ourselves; turn us, and we will be turned. Then, renew our days as of old, kekedem, as before.

teach.h: THE LAST VERSE: CAST OFF FOR GOOD?
teach.b: Now the hard part: that isn't the book's last verse. The last verse, in the same translation, reads: "Thou canst not have utterly rejected us, And be exceeding wroth against us!" The Hebrew is hard to pin down.
Those translators heard a protest: surely you haven't cast us off for good.
Other readers hear a plain statement that God has rejected them, or a fearful question left hanging. Either way, the book doesn't tie a bow. Jewish custom does something tender here.

When Lamentations is read aloud in public, the reader doesn't stop on the last verse. The plea before it is said again: turn us, renew our days. So the congregation closes the book not on that cry but on a request.
The custom doesn't change a word of the text. It changes where the voice comes to rest. Even the JPS 1917 printing sets the plea again, in brackets, after the last verse.
And the plea travels. When the Torah returns to the ark, the congregation sings hashivenu as the doors close.
A line from a city in ruins is sung over a scroll going home: a plea that has already been through the worst, and still asks.

how: When Lamentations is read aloud on Tisha B'Av, the next-to-last verse is repeated after the final one, and 'hashivenu' is sung in synagogue as the Torah scroll is returned to the ark.

o: we have returned home from the exile
turn us, bring us back: a plea to God
remember us, a plea not to be forgotten

games.q: renew our days — tap the pairs.
p: thou canst not have utterly rejected us

s: the very last verse is 'thou canst not have utterly rejected us.' the plea comes just before it.
when the book is read aloud, the plea is said again after the last verse
so the voice comes to rest on renewal, not rejection.
the custom changes the words of the book
every word is read. it only changes where the reading stops.

games.q: you're reading Lamentations aloud to a room of mourners. the last verse is a hard one to end on. what do you do?
o: stop there and close the book.
read it, then say the plea before it again.
games.why: that's the custom: read every word, then repeat 'turn us... renew our days,' so the book ends on a request.

practice: Think of one part of your life that has gone dry, a friendship, a habit you used to love, a way of paying attention that faded, and remember how it was when it was alive. Then ask for it to be renewed.
If you pray, use the verse itself: renew our days as of old.

wordCard.voice: Hashivenu. Turn us, bring us back: the plea near the end of Lamentations, asking God to renew our days, as of old. Today's word.
